source.title: QMix: Quality-Aware Learning With Mixed Noise for Robust Retinal Disease Diagnosis
source.authors: Jun-Lin Hou; Jilan Xu; Rui Feng; Hao Chen

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper qualitatively examines loss patterns across training and reports when correctly labeled and mislabeled samples are learned under label noise. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiment or measure its training and test errors.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses prior work on memorization, but cited results are not counted. Rows below capture its own described loss patterns in Fig. 4; other diagnosis scores under noisy datasets do not measure the behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Figure 4 reports the study's own training-loss trajectories in a retinal-image setting. These bear on V6: correctly labeled patterns are learned early, followed by memorization of incorrect high-quality-image labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the local loss observations but omits the main conclusion: QMix's joint uncertainty-loss separation and quality-aware semi-supervised training improve diagnosis robustness on six retinal datasets. The authors explain lower Mis-L loss through uncertain predictions, not earlier noisy-label learning, and acknowledge possible separation failures when disease features resemble low-quality-image artifacts.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies retinal disease diagnosis with synthetic and real-world mixed noise, using a QMix sample-separation and semi-supervised training framework; it does not use the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The described loss ordering differs between label noise only and mixed noise, where Mis-L has lower average loss than Mis-H.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-quality mislabeled images have lower early loss than mislabeled high-quality images because their predictions are approximately uniform and uncertain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image quality can disrupt loss-based identification of noisy labels without demonstrating earlier memorization of those labels.

record.problems: The memorization evidence is qualitative and the supplied description gives no numeric loss values or uncertainty estimates. Fig. 4's plotted curves are not numerically recoverable from the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the versions tested; other noisy-dataset diagnosis metrics do not measure training fit, random-label behavior, or the learning order named by the versions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and test error rising steadily from clean labels to completely random labels.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms clean-label generalization.

Fully random-label datasets and the temporal ordering of actual incorrect-label memorization for low-quality images. R2 establishes early learning of real patterns but does not explicitly establish subsequent memorization under mixed noise.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its qualitative loss trajectories support V6 in the tested conditions; diagnosis Kappa scores and sample-separation AUCs do not establish the other versions.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling experiment or training error and test error at chance are reported.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels, or convergence speed across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The paper varies mixed-noise ratios and reports diagnosis performance, but does not report perfect training fit and steadily rising test error as random label corruption increases.
No test of whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting or affect generalization on true labels.
The paper examines correctly labeled versus mislabeled samples, including mixed-noise cases, but does not test random labels or compare learned representations directly.

rows.subject: DNNs
rows.operation_detail: Describes loss patterns for Correct, Mis-H, and Mis-L during training under mixed noise.
rows.measure: Average loss pattern by sample type
rows.value: Correct is learned first; Mis-H has higher average loss than Mis-L in the early stage, while Mis-L has lower average loss than Mis-H.
rows.locator: Section III-A, Fig. 4(c) and accompanying text
rows.note: This supports an ordering for Correct and Mis-H, but the stated lower loss of Mis-L means the result does not establish that all noisy labels are learned only after real-label patterns.
rows.check: The early learning of Correct and higher loss on Mis-H support the tested early-learning component of V6. Lower loss on Mis-L does not establish earlier memorization: the authors attribute it to approximately uniform predictions on images lacking discriminative features. The extracted partial state and limits_scope verdict confuse lower loss with learning incorrect labels. Later memorization under mixed noise is not explicitly established by this row.
